content: The castor oil plant, scientifically known as Ricinus communis, belongs to the family Euphorbiaceae. It is the only species within the genus Ricinus and the subtribe Ricininae. The seeds of this plant, commonly referred to as castor beans, are not true beans despite their name. These seeds are the primary source of castor oil, which has a wide range of applications. Castor seeds contain between 40% and 60% oil, predominantly composed of triglycerides, with ricinolein being the main component. However, the seeds also contain ricin, a potent toxin, which is present in lower concentrations throughout the plant. The raw castor beans are highly toxic, and their ingestion can lead to severe poisoning. It is estimated that as few as three beans can be fatal to children, while adults may require the ingestion of eight or more beans to reach a lethal dose. Despite this, actual cases of poisoning are rare. For instance, in recent years, only two cases of castor bean poisoning have been reported in England, and both individuals recovered without complications. Historically, castor seeds have been discovered in Egyptian tombs dating back to 4000 BC. Ancient Greek travelers, including Herodotus, documented the use of castor seed oil for lighting and as a body ointment. Currently, global production of castor seeds is approximately one million tons annually, with India, China, and Brazil being the leading producers. Active breeding programs are in place to enhance the plant's cultivation and utility. The name Ricinus is derived from the Latin word for tick, as the seed's markings and shape resemble certain ticks. The common name castor oil likely originates from its historical use as a substitute for castoreum, a substance derived from the dried perineal glands of beavers (Castor in Latin). Another common name for the plant is Palm of Christ (Palma Christi), which refers to the oil's reputed healing properties for wounds and ailments. The castor oil plant is believed to be native to the southeastern Mediterranean region and Eastern Africa. Today, it is widely distributed across tropical regions and often establishes itself as a naturalized plant, particularly in wastelands. In Ethiopia, it is extensively cultivated as a crop. Additionally, the plant is frequently used as an ornamental species in parks and public spaces, often featured as a dot plant in traditional bedding schemes. The castor oil plant exhibits significant variability in its growth habit and appearance. It is a fast-growing, perennial shrub that can reach the size of a small tree, approximately 12 meters in height, in favorable conditions. However, it is not frost-hardy. In regions with frost, it is typically grown as an annual, reaching heights of 2–3 meters within a single growing season if started early under controlled conditions. The plant's glossy leaves are palmate, measuring 15–45 cm in length, with 5–12 deep lobes and toothed margins. Leaf coloration ranges from dark green, sometimes with a reddish hue, to dark reddish-purple or bronze. The stems and spiny seed pods also vary in pigmentation. The seed pods are more visually striking than the flowers, with male flowers being yellowish-green and bearing prominent creamy stamens, while female flowers at the tips of the spikes feature prominent red stigmas. Several cultivated varieties of the castor oil plant exist, including 'Gibsonii,' which grows to about 1.5–2 meters tall with reddish foliage and stems, brightest on young shoots; 'Red Spire,' which reaches 2–3 meters in height with red stems and bronze foliage; and 'Zanzibariensis,' a tall variety (2–3 meters) with large, mid-green leaves (up to 50 cm long) featuring white midribs. These height measurements refer to plants grown as annuals. The castor oil plant serves as a food source for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, such as the Giant Leopard Moth (Hypercompe scribonia), Hypercompe hambletoni, and The Nutmeg (Discestra trifolii). It is also a preferred food of the Tambourine Dove (Turtur tympanistria). In ethnobotany, the use of castor seed oil in India has been documented as far back as 2000 BC, primarily for lighting and as a medicinal agent. In traditional systems such as Unani, Ayurvedic, and other ethnomedical practices, it has been employed as a laxative, purgative, and cathartic. Similarly, in China, castor seed oil has been used for centuries in local medicine, both for internal applications and in dressings.
